summary: Argues that standards bodies working on protocols of mutual interest without formal coordination can cause serious problems, some of which may harm the Internet. It suggests that a robust process for joint development is needed. It is an informational IAB document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo argues that standards bodies must work together when they touch the same protocol, because two bodies can assign the same number to different things. It uses the abandoned T-MPLS work to show what goes wrong, and the joint MPLS-TP work to show what works better.

who is the design authority for a protocol
subtitle: Why two standards bodies writing the same protocol apart is a problem for the Internet.

tldr.problem: When two standards bodies develop a protocol of mutual interest without formal coordination, the same code point or the same protocol can end up meaning different things in each, which can harm the Internet as a whole.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the protocol design rules that miscoordination breaks, including the rule that the meaning of an allocated code point must never change, and that only one body should hold design authority for a protocol.
tldr.outcome: Development of the ITU-T's T-MPLS was abandoned because of conflicts with the IETF's MPLS, and the two bodies then created a joint working team that produced MPLS-TP together.

today: RFC 5704 is an Informational Internet Architecture Board memo published in November 2009, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the harm that uncoordinated protocol work caused and the joint working arrangement that the IETF and the ITU-T put in place for MPLS-TP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The uncoordinated adaptation of a protocol, parameter or code point by a standards development organization, either by allocating a code point without following the formal registration procedures or by unilaterally changing the meaning of the protocol or of the code point, poses a risk of harm to the Internet.

The Internet Architecture Board treats it as an essential principle of the protocol development process that only one standards development organization maintains design authority for a given protocol. That body has ultimate authority over the allocation of protocol parameter code points and over the intended semantics, interpretation and actions associated with those code points.

The case study is Transport MPLS, called T-MPLS, an ITU-T protocol for carrying packets over transport networks. Development of T-MPLS was abandoned by ITU-T Study Group 15 because of inherent conflicts with the IETF MPLS design and, in particular, with the Internet architecture. The conflicts arose from the lack of coordination with the IETF as the design authority for MPLS. At the time of writing, a joint IETF and ITU-T effort called the MPLS Transport Profile, MPLS-TP, was under way to extend MPLS in a way consistent with the MPLS architecture and with the requirements of the transport network provider.

The goal of the document is to demonstrate the importance of a coordinated approach and to explain a model for collaborative protocol development between standards bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo starts from a simple principle: one protocol should have one owner, and that owner decides what its numbers mean. When two bodies build on the same protocol without talking, the Internet ends up with two meanings for the same value.

sections.title: Protocol Design Rules
sections.content:
Many end users and businesses rely on the Internet as critical infrastructure, so an outage in a large-scale network causes significant commercial and political damage. When two incompatible protocols, or two incompatible forms of the same protocol, are deployed without coordination, there is a serious risk that this is catastrophic to the stability or security of the network. The scale and distributed nature of the Internet make it difficult or impossible to rid the network of the long-term consequences of such an incompatibility.

Three rules explain why. The first is the importance of invariants, which are core properties that stay consistent across the network and do not change over extremely long time scales. Designers use invariants as axioms, and a protocol often relies absolutely on one to settle a corner case. An example inherited from IP into MPLS is that a time to live value decreases monotonically and that a packet with a time to live of one or less is not forwarded, which limits the damage of forwarding loops. Another example is the way MPLS gives special semantics to the reserved label set, 0 to 15, leaving label switching routers free to allocate labels of 16 or greater for their own use.

The second rule is the importance of correct identification. A code point identifies a packet type or a component within a packet, and without such identifiers a packet is an opaque sequence of bits. A parser first identifies the code point and then uses the associated semantics to interpret the rest of the packet. Once a code point is defined, the interpretation of the associated data and the consequential actions become invariants that later protocol development must follow. The semantics for an allocated code point must never change: if a future enhancement needs different semantics, interpretation or action, then a new code point must be obtained.

The third rule is the role of the design authority. A code point such as an IEEE Ethertype is allocated to a design authority such as the IETF, which establishes how the information identified by that code point is to be interpreted. Modifying and extending a protocol requires great care, because the exact nature of the invariants and the consequences of modification have to be understood, and that understanding may not be available to an organization that did not write the original protocol. Because there can only safely be a single interpretation of a code point, there must be a unique authority responsible for authorising and documenting its semantics and the protocol actions that follow. The IETF has such a process for the protocols where it holds design authority, and a change process for working with other bodies. The memo recommends that the IETF introduce additional change mechanisms covering all the technical areas where it holds design authority.

A fourth point is often used to justify an uncoordinated change: the claim that the two variants of a protocol will never meet, because they operate in different parts of the network and never need to interoperate. The memo calls this a ships in the night assumption and rejects it. It is infeasible to ensure that the two instances will never be interconnected under any circumstances, and even where operators apply due diligence it is infeasible to ensure that conflicting protocols are not interconnected under fault conditions. The assumption is particularly hazardous when the two variants share the same identifying code point, because a system cannot then tell which variant it has received and so cannot know how to interpret the information or which actions are safe.
sections.plainLanguage: Some properties of a protocol are treated as fixed rules, such as a packet's time to live only ever going down. Once a number has been given a meaning, that meaning must never change; a different meaning needs a different number. One organisation should own each protocol so that it can enforce this.

sections.title: Examples of Miscoordination
sections.content:
T-MPLS was created in the ITU-T to design a packet transport method for transport-oriented networks, and the document treats it as a case study of a protocol built on misunderstandings of IETF protocols. Quite late in the ITU-T design and specification cycle there were a number of liaison exchanges with the IETF, in which the IETF became increasingly concerned about incompatibility between IETF MPLS procedures and ITU-T T-MPLS. Extensive discussions took place over interpretation, definition and misunderstandings concerning MPLS label 14, the MPLS swap operation, time to live semantics, the reservation of additional labels and the EXP bits. If the ITU-T had worked with the IETF from the start, the memo says, these problems could have been avoided.

The second case is the other direction: an example where the IETF failed to coordinate with the ITU-T. PPP over SONET, defined in RFC 1619, stated in the section on the SONET and SDH Synchronous Payload Envelope that no scrambling is needed during insertion into that envelope. SONET experts in the ITU-T and ANSI later determined that the error came from an incomplete understanding of the SONET scrambler. Without a scrambler, the protocol was attempting to transport non-transparent data over SONET, which resulted in lost or misinterpreted data in the packet over SONET network, affecting routing, signalling and end-user traffic. The problem was resolved by working jointly with ITU-T and ANSI experts to publish RFC 2615, which mandated the use of scrambling. The memo notes that RFC 1619 was developed four years before the IETF and the ITU-T agreed on formal cooperation procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Two worked examples. The ITU-T built T-MPLS without the IETF and the two versions of MPLS ended up conflicting. The IETF once described how to carry packets over SONET without asking the SONET experts, and got the scrambling wrong until the two sides worked together.

sections.title: Managing Information Flow
sections.content:
The memo recommends that information flows inside and between standards bodies be managed carefully, to prevent the accidental extension of protocols without complete coordination with the relevant design authority.

Within a standards body, one cannot assume that another body is familiar with its internal structure, information exchange or internal processes. The initial contact point, and the subgroup with which a long-term working relationship is formed, therefore has a duty to make sure that the work is fully notified and coordinated with all relevant parties inside that body.

Between standards bodies, the recommendation is that as part of their document approval process, bodies should confirm that all protocol parameters, code points and TLV identifiers have been authorised by the appropriate design authority, such as IANA or the IETF, and that approval from the design authority has been obtained before publishing protocol extensions. This confirmation should be an integral part of the approval or consent process, verifying that the normative references are qualified.
sections.plainLanguage: Before publishing an extension, a standards body should check that the numbers it uses were properly allocated by the body that owns the protocol, and should record that check as part of its own approval process.

sections.title: MPLS-TP as Best Practice
sections.content:
To close the gap between the two organizations, the IETF and the ITU-T established a joint working team to assess whether existing MPLS standards could be enhanced to provide a best-in-class solution for transport networks. The outcome of that investigation is reported in RFC 5317. The team proposed a design acceptable to both bodies, which led to the creation of the MPLS-TP project, a joint project in which ITU-T experts work with the IETF on protocol development tasks and IETF members work within the ITU-T to understand requirements and to help create the ITU-T recommendations that describe MPLS-TP, with the technical definition provided through normative references to IETF RFCs.

The memo is candid about the cost of that approach. The joint working team required considerable protocol design expertise and IETF management time to agree on a suitable technical solution. A lighter process, starting with close coordination during the requirements phase and continuing during the development phase, would likely reduce the resources needed to an acceptable level in the future.

The memo also notes that the IETF has a change process for MPLS, defined in RFC 4929, but has not defined one that applies to all of its work areas, and argues that the problems described here show that the IETF needs to develop a universal change process, with the MPLS change process a suitable starting point.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix the memo describes is a joint team: both bodies work on the transport profile together, and the ITU-T recommendation points at IETF documents for the technical detail. It costs a lot of effort, and the memo argues that coordinating earlier would cost less.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The uncoordinated development of protocols poses a risk of harm to the Internet and must not be permitted. Enhancing or modifying a protocol can increase attack surfaces considerably and may therefore compromise the security or stability of the Internet.

The IETF has a review process that combines cross-area review with specialist security review by experts familiar with the development and deployment context of the Internet protocol suite. Because the Internet infrastructure relies on the IP and MPLS protocol suites, this review must be exercised with considerable diligence. Failing to apply it exposes the Internet to increased risk along both security and stability lines.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a protocol without review opens new ways to attack it, which is why the review process the IETF applies to its own work matters here.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT UNCOORDINATED WORK BREAKS

items.title: Safety
items.text: Incompatible forms of the same protocol deployed together can be catastrophic to the network's stability and security.

items.title: Invariants
items.text: Core properties, such as a time to live that only ever decreases, are relied on to handle corner cases.

items.title: Correct identification
items.text: The meaning of an allocated code point must never change; a new meaning needs a new code point.

items.title: One design authority
items.text: A single body must authorise and document what a code point means and what actions follow.
